title: Secured network edge: ACLs, NAT/PAT, SSH-only management and port security
summary: Harden a small network's edge and access layer: PAT to the internet, static NAT for a server, ACLs that enforce a written policy, SSH-only management and port security.
why: Security is part of every network job. This shows you can turn a security policy into working configuration and prove each rule with a test, which is what reviewers look for in a junior network or security candidate.
brief:
Start from the small-office network (or build something similar) and add an edge router connected to a simulated ISP with a test server on the internet side, plus an internal web server. Write a one-page security policy first, then implement and test it. An example policy: staff can reach the internet and the internal server; guests can reach only the internet; only the management VLAN can SSH to network devices; the internal web server is reachable from the internet on HTTPS only; everything else is denied.

Implement PAT (NAT overload) so all inside hosts share the edge router's public address, and a static NAT mapping for the internal server. Write named extended ACLs that enforce the policy, placed close to the source, with a remark on every entry. Lock down management: local user accounts with hashed secrets, SSH version 2 only with a 2048-bit RSA key, `transport input ssh` on the VTY lines with an access-class that allows only the management subnet, an exec timeout, a login banner, and no Telnet. On the access switches, enable port security (a maximum MAC count, sticky learning and a chosen violation mode) and, if your simulator supports it, DHCP snooping with trusted uplinks.

Every policy statement needs a test: a table of source, destination, port, expected result and observed result, with ACL hit counters as evidence.

milestones.title: Policy and plan
tasks: Write the security policy as numbered, testable statements
List the ACLs needed, their entries, and the interface and direction for each
Plan the inside local and inside global addresses for NAT
milestones.doneWhen: A policy document maps every statement to the ACL entry or feature that will enforce it.

milestones.title: NAT and PAT
tasks: Mark the ip nat inside and ip nat outside interfaces
Configure PAT with an ACL and the overload keyword
Add a static NAT mapping for the internal server
milestones.doneWhen: `show ip nat translations` shows several inside hosts sharing one public address and the static entry for the server, and inside hosts reach the ISP test server.

milestones.title: ACLs
tasks: Write named extended ACLs with a remark for each policy statement
Apply each one on the right interface in the right direction
Account for the implicit deny, adding explicit permits for traffic the policy allows (such as DHCP and replies)
milestones.doneWhen: Every row of the policy test table passes, and `show access-lists` shows matches on the entries each test should hit.

milestones.title: Management hardening
tasks: Configure a hostname, domain name, a 2048-bit RSA key, ip ssh version 2 and local users with secret passwords
Set transport input ssh, login local, an access-class and exec-timeout on the VTY lines
Add a login banner and service password-encryption, and disable services you do not use
milestones.doneWhen: SSH from the management VLAN succeeds, while Telnet from anywhere and SSH from a user VLAN both fail.

milestones.title: Access-layer security
tasks: Enable port security with a maximum of 2 MACs, sticky learning and the restrict or shutdown violation mode
Trigger a violation by connecting an extra device, and record the counters
Enable DHCP snooping with trusted uplinks if supported, and test it with a rogue DHCP server
milestones.doneWhen: `show port-security interface` shows the violation from your test, and the port behaved as its violation mode says.

milestones.title: Audit report
tasks: Complete the test table with expected and observed results for every policy statement
Save the show output used as evidence
Write a short section on remaining risks and what you would add next
milestones.doneWhen: The report shows every policy statement tested with evidence and lists at least three remaining risks.

stretch: Send logs to a syslog server and match an ACL deny to its log entry
Add NTP so log timestamps are accurate
Add AAA with a RADIUS or TACACS+ server
Write an IPv6 ACL that enforces the same policy
rubric: A reviewer should see a written policy in which every statement maps to specific configuration and a test
A reviewer should see named extended ACLs with remarks, placed near the source and applied in the correct direction
A reviewer should see PAT translating many hosts and a static NAT entry for the server
A reviewer should see SSH version 2 only, local authentication, a VTY access-class and Telnet refused
A reviewer should see port security tested with a real violation and its counters
A reviewer should see a test table with expected and observed results backed by saved show output
A reviewer should see published configurations with passwords and secrets removed or replaced
showcase: Create a GitHub repository with the policy document, sanitized per-device configs, the test table and evidence, and the topology diagram
Put the policy-to-test table at the top of the README; it shows security thinking at a glance
Keep the 'Remaining risks' section: it shows judgment beyond following steps
Sanitize configs before publishing by removing password hashes, keys and any real addresses
resumeBullet: Hardened a small-office network in Packet Tracer with PAT, static NAT, extended ACLs enforcing a written security policy, SSH-only management and port security; verified all 15 policy rules with a documented test matrix.
interviewTalkingPoints: Where you placed each ACL and why extended ACLs go close to the source
How PAT lets many hosts share one address, and what the translation table shows
The differences between the protect, restrict and shutdown violation modes, and which you chose
Why SSH with an access-class is far stronger than a password on the VTY lines
A rule that failed at first, and how ACL hit counters helped you find the cause
